function pyReprStr(s) {
  const cps = [...s];
  const hasSq = cps.includes("'"), hasDq = cps.includes('"');
  const q = (hasSq && !hasDq) ? '"' : "'";
  let out = q;
  for (const ch of cps) {
    const cp = ch.codePointAt(0);
    if (ch === '\\')      out += '\\\\';
    else if (ch === q)    out += '\\' + q;
    else if (cp === 0x09) out += '\\t';
    else if (cp === 0x0a) out += '\\n';
    else if (cp === 0x0d) out += '\\r';
    else if (isPyPrintable(cp)) out += ch;          // Unicode 15.0 GC not in {Cc,Cf,Cs,Co,Cn,Zl,Zp,Zs}, plus U+0020
    else if (cp <= 0xff)   out += '\\x' + cp.toString(16).padStart(2,'0');
    else if (cp <= 0xffff) out += '\\u' + cp.toString(16).padStart(4,'0');
    else                   out += '\\U' + cp.toString(16).padStart(8,'0');
  }
  return out + q;
}
function pyReprDict(entries) {
  return '{' + entries.map(([k,v]) => pyReprStr(k) + ': ' + pyReprStr(v)).join(', ') + '}';
}

verdicts.note: Mispredicts any tail that begins with one or more extra 'h' characters, because argparse re-enters the single-dash unpacking loop and re-splits the remaining tail. Counterexamples (all exit 2, stdout empty): `/workspace/dataset/test8_executable -hh=x` -> `test8_executable: error: argument -h/--help: ignored explicit argument 'x'` (rule predicts help, since tail `h=x` does not start with '-' and the top-level split was not on '='); `-hhh=x` -> same, `'x'`; `-hh=` -> `ignored explicit argument ''`; `-hh-x` -> `ignored explicit argument '-x'` (rule predicts help). Meanwhile these DO print help, exit 0: `-hx=y`, `-h0=1`, `-hh1=2`, `-hhx=y`, `-hh`, `-hhh`, `-hhx`, `-hxh=y`, `-hha`, `-hfoo`, `-h1`, `-h `. Correct mechanical rule (single-dash peel loop), for opt='-h', sep and expl from classification: loop { if expl===null -> run help, exit 0; if expl==='' -> error `ignored explicit argument ''`; if sep==='=' || expl[0]==='-' -> error `ignored explicit argument '<expl>'`; if ('-'+expl[0]) is not a known option ('-h' is the only one) -> run help, exit 0; else expl=expl.slice(1); if expl==='' {expl=null; sep=null} else if (expl[0]==='=') {sep='='; expl=expl.slice(1)} else {sep=''} }. The reference JS in the notes implements only one pass and therefore prints help for `-hh=x` / `-hh-x`. Confirmed unchanged: `-h=`, `-h=x`, `-h-x`, `-h--`, `-h-1`, `--help=1`, `--help=`, `--h=1` -> error; error text always names the action `-h/--help`.

verdicts.rule: OPTION=VALUE always bypasses classification of the value (`--payload=-x`, `--payload=x=y`, `--payload=`).
verdicts.note: All exit 0: `--payload=-x --secret s` -> `{'data': '-x'}`; `--payload=x=y --secret s` -> `{'data': 'x=y'}` (split at first '=' only); `--payload= --secret=` -> `{'data': ''}`; `--payload=-- --secret s` -> `{'data': '--'}`. Minor overstatement in the last clause: it is not the ONLY way to pass an option-looking string — a separate token also works if it contains U+0020 (`--payload '-x y'`) or matches the negative-number regex (`--payload -1`).

verdicts.rule: Line 2 is the Python repr of the claims dict: single quotes normally, double quotes if the value contains ' and no "; non-ASCII emitted raw UTF-8.
verdicts.note: `--payload "it's" --secret s` -> `{'data': "it's"}`; `--payload 'a"b'` -> `{'data': 'a"b'}`; both quote types present -> single quotes with backslash escape: `--payload 'a'\''b"c'` -> `{'data': 'a\'b"c'}`; control chars are escaped: a literal TAB in the payload prints `{'data': 'a\tb'}`; backslashes doubled; `--payload 'héllo→'` -> `{'data': 'héllo→'}` raw UTF-8; `--payload -١` -> cat -A shows `{'data': '-M-YM-!'}` i.e. raw U+0661 bytes.

verdicts.rule: HELP TEXT (byte-exact). `--help` writes exactly these 164 bytes to STDOUT and exits 0 ... help column at 0-based index 21.
verdicts.note: Reproduced byte-for-byte. `cd /workspace/dataset && ./test8_executable --help >/tmp/h.out 2>/tmp/h.err` -> EXIT=0, stdout 164 bytes, stderr 0 bytes; `od -An -c /tmp/h.out` matches their dump exactly (L1=62,L2=0,L3=8,L4=52,L5=19,L6=17; 9 spaces between '--help' and 'show'). Caveat (covered by their rule 18, not a defect here): the 164-byte form only holds when the effective terminal width is >= 64, i.e. COLUMNS unset, empty, non-numeric, 0, negative, or >= 64. `COLUMNS=40 ./test8_executable --help` emits 207 bytes with a wrapped usage AND a re-flowed options block.

verdicts.rule: STREAMS. Help only to stdout (stderr empty); all errors (usage+error) only to stderr (stdout empty); success output to stdout.
verdicts.note: Could not break it. Across ~90 invocations (help forms, all error classes, success) stdout and stderr were never both non-empty. e.g. `./test8_executable -h >/tmp/o 2>/tmp/e` -> o=164 e=0; `./test8_executable --payload x --secret y --pz >/tmp/o 2>/tmp/e` -> o=0, e=usage+error; `./test8_executable --payload x --secret y >/tmp/o 2>/tmp/e` -> o=3 lines, e=0.

verdicts.rule: ERROR ENVELOPE. Every parse error prints EXACTLY two lines to stderr and exits 2; line 1 identical to help line 1; the error line is NEVER wrapped even when terminal width is small.
verdicts.note:
Two sub-claims are wrong at narrow widths, and their own COLUMNS=40 evidence already contradicts the 'exactly two lines' wording. `COLUMNS=20 ./test8_executable 2>&1 >/dev/null` prints SEVEN lines:
usage: test8_executable
       [-h]
       --payload
       PAYLOAD
       --secret
       SECRET
test8_executable: error: the following arguments are required: --payload, --secret

Corrected rule: stderr = render_usage(width) + one unwrapped 'PROG: error: MSG
' line, exit 2. The usage block is wrapped by the same width logic as help (single line only when effective width >= 62, i.e. COLUMNS >= 64 or unset). The 'never wrapped' part of the error line IS confirmed: `COLUMNS=20 ./test8_executable --payload a --secret b aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa bbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbb 2>&1 >/dev/null` emits the 110-char 'unrecognized arguments: aaaa... bbbb...' line intact on one line.

verdicts.rule: MISSING REQUIRED. Message = 'the following arguments are required: ' + canonical long names joined by ', ' in declaration order (--payload before --secret) regardless of argv order. Exit 2.
verdicts.note: Reproduced with no args, `--payload x`, `--secret y`, and also with reversed/abbreviated/unknown forms: `./test8_executable --secret y` -> '... required: --payload'; `./test8_executable --pz x --secret y` -> '... required: --payload'; `./test8_executable --Payload x --secret y` -> '... required: --payload' (matching is case-sensitive); `./test8_executable ---help` and `--HELP` and `-H` -> '... required: --payload, --secret'. All exit 2.

verdicts.rule: ABBREVIATION RESOLVES. Any non-empty prefix of exactly one long option resolves to it; every prefix is unambiguous because h/p/s are distinct; prefixes work with '=' too.
verdicts.note: Re-ran the full prefix matrix plus '=' forms: `--p=x --s=y`, `--p= --s=`, `--h`, `--he`, `--hel` all behave as claimed (exit 0). No 1+-character long prefix is ambiguous. Worth adding for a JS port: single-dash prefix matching also exists and is what makes '-hx' work ('-h' is matched as short_option_prefix), but no single-dash prefix of a LONG option matches — `./test8_executable --payload a --secret b -p` -> 'unrecognized arguments: -p', i.e. '-p' does NOT abbreviate '--payload'.

verdicts.rule: ABBREVIATION NON-PREFIX = UNKNOWN. '--pz', '--paz', '--sekret', '--bogus', etc. become unrecognized extras; if that leaves a required option unset you get the 'required' error.
verdicts.note: Reproduced exactly. Extra cases: `./test8_executable --payload x --pz y --secret z` -> 'unrecognized arguments: --pz y' (the unknown option AND its would-be value both become extras); `./test8_executable ---` and `---help` -> 'required: --payload, --secret' (three dashes is just an unknown long option, never an abbreviation).

verdicts.rule: AMBIGUITY. The ONLY reachable ambiguous case is a token starting with '--' whose name part before '=' is empty ('--=', '--=1', '--=abc'); message echoes the FULL token; candidates '--help, --payload, --secret'. Bare '--' is not ambiguous.
verdicts.note:
Message format and candidate list confirmed, including `--=a=b` and `--==` -> 'ambiguous option: --=a=b could match --help, --payload, --secret' / '... --== ...'. Two corrections:
(1) It mispredicts tokens after a '--' separator. `./test8_executable -- --=1` -> exit 2 'the following arguments are required: --payload, --secret' (NOT ambiguous), and `./test8_executable --payload a --secret b -- --=1` -> 'unrecognized arguments: -- --=1'. Everything after the first bare '--' is forced positional and never option-parsed.
(2) The ambiguity check runs in a PRE-SCAN over all argv tokens before any action executes, so it beats every other outcome including help: `./test8_executable -h --=` -> exit 2 ambiguous (stdout empty), and `./test8_executable --payload --=1` -> exit 2 ambiguous (not 'expected one argument'). Note also the candidate list only contains options starting with '--' ('-h' is excluded) because the matched prefix is literally '--'.

verdicts.rule: '=' SYNTAX for value-taking options. Split on the FIRST '=' only; '--payload=' / '--secret=' set the empty string; abbreviations accept '='.
verdicts.note: Reproduced plus: `./test8_executable --payload=x=y=z --secret=` -> exit 0, {'data': 'x=y=z'}; `./test8_executable --p= --s=` -> exit 0, {'data': ''}. Also worth stating explicitly for a port: with '=' the value may start with '-' — `./test8_executable --payload=-x --secret y` -> {'data': '-x'}, `--payload=--` -> {'data': '--'}, `--payload=-h` -> {'data': '-h'}, all exit 0.

verdicts.rule: '=' WITH HELP. Any help spelling with an explicit '=' value errors: "argument -h/--help: ignored explicit argument '<VALUE>'", value in Python repr single quotes. Exit 2.
verdicts.note: Reproduced --help=1 / --h=1 / --he=1 / --hel=1 / -h=1. Additional boundary cases that follow the same rule: `./test8_executable --help=` and `-h=` and `--h=` -> "ignored explicit argument ''" (empty repr, two quote chars); `-h==` -> "ignored explicit argument '='" (split on first '=' only). Also confirmed this error is NOT pre-scanned: `./test8_executable -h --help=1` -> exit 0, help printed, because the earlier -h action fires first.

verdicts.rule: '=' ON AN UNKNOWN OPTION. Whole token including '=1' echoed as one unrecognized token; 'required' wins if a required option is unset.
verdicts.note: Reproduced --unknown=1 and --pz=1 in both configurations. Also `./test8_executable --payload x --secret y --s=q --pz` -> 'unrecognized arguments: --pz' (the valid abbreviation --s=q is consumed, only the unknown token is echoed).

verdicts.rule: PRECEDENCE: 'required' BEATS 'unrecognized arguments'.
verdicts.note: Reproduced all six of their cases. Additional: `./test8_executable --pz x --secret y` -> required --payload (the extras --pz and x are silently dropped from the message); `./test8_executable -- -h` -> required --payload, --secret. Caveat already implied elsewhere: both are outranked by ambiguous-option (pre-scan) and by 'expected one argument' (raised mid-scan).

verdicts.rule: UNRECOGNIZED ARGUMENTS. 'unrecognized arguments: ' + leftovers joined by a single space in original argv order; '--' itself included; empty-string argv element contributes an empty token. Exit 2.
verdicts.note: Could not find any reordering counterexample. Verified argv-order preservation with mixed positional/unknown-option interleavings: `./test8_executable gamma --alpha --payload a --secret b --beta` -> 'gamma --alpha --beta'; `./test8_executable --alpha --payload a --secret b --beta gamma` -> '--alpha --beta gamma'; `./test8_executable --payload a --secret b extra -- more` -> 'extra -- more'; `-- -- extra` -> '-- -- extra'. Trailing-space claim verified byte-wise: `./test8_executable --payload a --secret b '' 2>/tmp/e` then `od -An -c /tmp/e` ends '... a r g u m e n t s :  (space) \n'; with two empty strings it ends with two spaces before \n. Also '-', '---', '-p', '-1', '-1x' all land in extras verbatim.

verdicts.rule: MISSING VALUE / VALUE LOOKS LIKE AN OPTION. Triggered when the option is the last token, or when the next token starts with '-' and is not a negative number. '-1' IS accepted.
verdicts.note:
The 'starts with - and is not a negative number' predicate mispredicts at least three input classes (all exit 0, all should be errors under the stated rule):
  `./test8_executable --payload - --secret y` -> exit 0, {'data': '-'}  (a lone '-' is always a value)
  `./test8_executable --payload '-x y' --secret y` -> exit 0, {'data': '-x y'}  (token contains a space and matches no option prefix -> value)
  `./test8_executable --payload '- x' --secret y` -> exit 0, {'data': '- x'}; `--payload '-1 '` -> {'data': '-1 '}; `--payload ' -1'` -> {'data': ' -1'}
  `./test8_executable --payload -.5 --secret y` -> exit 0, {'data': '-.5'}  ('-.5' has no digit before the dot yet is still 'negative-number-like')
Corrected predicate: the following token IS consumed as a value iff it is the empty string, OR its first char is not '-', OR it is exactly '-', OR it matches /^-\d+$/ or /^-\d*\.\d+$/, OR (it matches no registered option/prefix AND contains a space). Otherwise -> 'argument <CANONICAL>: expected one argument'. Confirmed errors: `--payload -1a`, `--payload -secret`, `--payload --`, `--payload -h`, `--payload -x`, and bare trailing `--payload`/`--p`/`--s`.
Also the precedence claim needs one exception: this error does NOT beat the ambiguous-option pre-scan — `./test8_executable --payload --=1` -> exit 2 'ambiguous option: --=1 could match --help, --payload, --secret'.
The canonical-name part IS confirmed: `--p` and `--payload x --secret y --p` both report 'argument --payload: expected one argument'.

verdicts.rule: HELP WINS OVER MISSING-REQUIRED AND OVER UNKNOWN OPTIONS. If -h/--help/--h/--he/--hel appears anywhere and is REACHED in the left-to-right scan, help prints to stdout and exit 0.
verdicts.note:
Falsified by the ambiguous-option pre-scan, which runs over ALL argv tokens before any action executes, so an ambiguous token anywhere (even far to the RIGHT of -h) kills help:
  `./test8_executable -h '--='` -> EXIT=2, stdout EMPTY, stderr 'usage: ...\ntest8_executable: error: ambiguous option: --= could match --help, --payload, --secret'
  `./test8_executable --help '--=1'` -> EXIT=2, same class of error
  `./test8_executable -h -h '--='` -> EXIT=2 ambiguous
  `./test8_executable -h --payload=x --secret=y '--=q'` -> EXIT=2 'ambiguous option: --=q could match ...'
  `./test8_executable --payload x --secret y -h '--=zzz'` -> EXIT=2 ambiguous
Corrected rule: FIRST classify every token left-to-right until a bare '--'; if any of them is an ambiguous long-option prefix, error immediately (exit 2). ONLY THEN execute actions left-to-right, where -h/--help/--h/--he/--hel/-hX fires help and exits 0, beating missing-required and unknown options. Their other listed cases all reproduce: `--bogus -h`, `-h --bogus`, `--payload x -h`, `--bogus=1 -h`, `--help --payload`, `--payload x --help --secret`, `-h -- --payload`, `--payload x -h y` -> all exit 0 with the 164-byte help; `--payload -h`, `--help=1 -h` -> exit 2; `-- -h` -> exit 2 required error.

verdicts.rule: SHORT-OPTION CLUSTER '-hX'. '-h' + non-'-' chars fires help and exits 0; if the trailing char is '-' it errors with "ignored explicit argument '-'"; '-xh'/'-x' never fire help.
verdicts.note:
Direction is right but the error message is misstated for multi-char tails: the reported value is the ENTIRE remainder after '-h', not a single '-'.
  `./test8_executable -h-x` -> exit 2, "argument -h/--help: ignored explicit argument '-x'"
  `./test8_executable -h--`  -> exit 2, "... ignored explicit argument '--'"
  `./test8_executable -h-h`  -> exit 2, "... ignored explicit argument '-h'"
Corrected rule: for a token '-h'+TAIL with no '=', if TAIL[0] is a prefix char ('-') the parser errors with "argument -h/--help: ignored explicit argument '<TAIL>'"; otherwise the whole TAIL is discarded and help fires (exit 0). Additional confirmations of the help branch: `-he`, `-h1`, `-hpayload`, and even `'-h '` (trailing space) all print the 164-byte help and exit 0 — note '-h ' fires help even though a space normally forces a token to be positional, because short-prefix matching happens before the space check. `-xh`/`-x` confirmed as plain extras.

verdicts.rule: LAST-WINS FOR REPEATED OPTIONS; ORDER-INDEPENDENT.
verdicts.note: Reproduced, plus mixed canonical/abbreviated repeats: `./test8_executable --payload a --p b --secret y` -> {'data': 'b'} (same token as their --payload a --payload b case); `./test8_executable --secret a --secret b --payload p` -> exit 0, signature differs from the --secret a variant, i.e. the LAST --secret wins too.

verdicts.rule: PROG NAME IS DYNAMIC: basename(argv[0]) in both the usage line and the 'PROG: error:' prefix.
verdicts.note: Stronger evidence than a copy: it tracks argv[0], not the on-disk file. `bash -c 'exec -a fakeprog /tmp/zz_renamed_prog --help'` -> 'usage: fakeprog [-h] --payload PAYLOAD --secret SECRET'; a symlink `/tmp/linkname_prog -> /tmp/zz_renamed_prog` -> 'usage: linkname_prog ...'; invoking via absolute path `/workspace/dataset/test8_executable` still yields prog 'test8_executable' (basename, not the full path).

verdicts.rule: WRAPPING WIDTH = COLUMNS - 2 (fallback 80 -> width 78); usage single-line for COLUMNS>=64, wraps for <=63; continuation indent 24; at COLUMNS=40 help column is 18 and the help text wraps; error line never wrapped.
verdicts.note:
Rule text is correct and I reproduced every part, BUT their pasted observedStdout for COLUMNS=40 (in this rule and in rule 3) is fabricated/wrong: it shows the options block unchanged. Real output of `COLUMNS=40 ./test8_executable --help`:
  options:
  -h, --help      show this help
                  message and exit
  --payload PAYLOAD
  --secret SECRET

(help column measured at 0-based 18 via awk index). Threshold re-verified: COLUMNS=61/62/63 wrap, 64/65 do not. Extra edges a JS port may want: COLUMNS=0, negative ('-5'), non-numeric ('abc') and empty all fall back to width 78 (identical 164-byte help); the layout saturates for small values — COLUMNS=1 through 17 all produce identical output (help text wrapped at 11 columns: 'show this'/'help'/'message and'/'exit'), COLUMNS=18 starts differing.

verdicts.rule: SUCCESS PATH. Exit 0, three stdout lines: token, Python dict repr of claims with single quotes, then {'alg': 'HS256', 'typ': 'JWT'}. Non-ASCII escaped as \uXXXX in the JWT but printed raw UTF-8 in the repr; tabs print as '\t'.
verdicts.note:
The 'single quotes' part is wrong for values containing an apostrophe — Python repr switches to double quotes:
  `./test8_executable --payload "it's" --secret s` -> line 2 is  {'data': "it's"}
  `./test8_executable --payload "both ' and \"" --secret s` -> line 2 is  {'data': 'both \' and "'}  (both quote kinds present -> single quotes with backslash-escaped apostrophe)
  `./test8_executable --payload 'say "hi"' --secret s` -> {'data': 'say "hi"'} (double quote alone does NOT change the delimiter)
Corrected rule for line 2/3 value rendering: use Python str repr — delimiter is ' unless the string contains ' and does not contain ", in which case it is "; inside a '-delimited string a literal ' is escaped as \'; \\ is always escaped as \\\\; \n/\r/\t render as the two-char escapes; other C0 controls render as \xNN (`--payload $'a\x01b'` -> {'data': 'a\x01b'}); printable non-ASCII is emitted raw UTF-8.
Everything else confirmed, plus astral characters in the JWT use UTF-16 surrogate escapes: `--payload '😀'` -> JWT payload segment decodes to {"data": "😀"} while the repr line prints the raw emoji bytes.

verdicts.rule: The golden vector file exists at /tmp/golden_vectors.tsv with exactly 73 lines (17195 bytes), 4 tab-separated fields per line: payload<TAB>secret<TAB>base64url_signature<TAB>full_token. A companion file /tmp/golden_vectors_ctl.tsv holds 9 additional vectors whose payload/secret contain TAB/LF/CR (fields 1-2 are C-escaped there).
verdicts.note: Reproduced exactly. `wc -l -c /tmp/golden_vectors.tsv /tmp/golden_vectors_ctl.tsv` -> `73 17195` and `9 1416`. `awk -F'\t' '{print NF}' | sort | uniq -c` -> `73 4` for the main file and `9 4` for the ctl file (the ctl file also has 4 fields, not stated but true). Raw tab count per line is exactly 3 on every line (`awk '{n=gsub(/\t/,"\t"); print n}' | sort | uniq -c` -> `73 3`), and the file ends in a single LF (`tail -c 1 | od -c` -> `\n`). I round-tripped the ctl file myself by C-unescaping fields 1-2 with `printf '%b'` and re-running the executable: 9/9 tokens matched. One latent hazard worth noting: the C-unescape is ambiguous for a literal backslash, and the ctl file happens to contain no backslash payloads, so it works — but the MAIN file DOES contain literal-backslash payloads (rows 47-48), so a harness must NOT apply the unescaper to the main file.

verdicts.rule: Every line has exactly 4 tab-delimited fields, every signature is exactly 43 base64url characters matching /^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$/ (no '=' padding, no '+', no '/'), every token has exactly 3 dot-separated segments, and no field contains a CR byte.
verdicts.note: Reproduced verbatim: field-count histogram `73 4`; signature-length histogram `73 43`; `split($4,a,".")` yields `3` for all rows; zero charset violations; `grep -c $'\r'` -> 0. I additionally verified field 3 is byte-identical to the substring of field 4 after the second dot on all 73 rows (`awk -F'\t' '{n=split($4,a,"."); if (a[3]!=$3) print NR}'` printed nothing). I also tried to break the 43-char/no-padding invariant with a 3000-byte payload AND 3000-byte secret: `--payload=ZZZ...(3000) --secret=ZZZ...(3000)` gave seg1len=36 seg2len=4015 seg3len=43, no '=' padding and no line wrapping. Output is deterministic (same input 3x -> 1 distinct token), so there is no iat/nonce.

verdicts.rule: The file is self-consistent: re-running the executable with each row's payload and secret reproduces field 4 (full_token) and field 3 (signature) byte-for-byte, for all 73 of 73 rows. A JS reimplementation is correct iff it reproduces both fields for every row.
verdicts.note: The self-consistency half is CONFIRMED — I independently re-ran the exact-split round-trip and got `FINAL ROUNDTRIP: lines=73 ok=73 bad=0`, and separately wrote a from-scratch Node reimplementation (/tmp/adv_check.js) that reproduces field 4 on 73/73 main rows and 9/9 ctl rows. But the 'iff' is FALSE: passing all 73 rows is necessary, not sufficient. Counterexample — byte 0x08 appears nowhere in the golden file (`grep -c $'\x08' /tmp/golden_vectors.tsv` -> 0), yet the executable escapes it as the short form \b. `/workspace/dataset/test8_executable --payload=$'a\bb' --secret=k` -> `eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJkYXRhIjoiYVxiYiJ9.FpAqyv_JZotaLjFzO6M8If0C1lhK8RHnpODonx8Qv7w` (seg2 = {"data":"a\bb"}), whereas a  -emitting implementation produces `...eyJkYXRhIjoiYVx1MDAwOGIifQ._L-ey9-LStD7pKnef7st7z_wck3PzY6ZGYQTd42zqaQ`. That implementation still scores 73/73 on the file. A second uncovered class: invalid UTF-8 in the secret makes the program EXIT 1 with a traceback (see rule-8/rule-15 notes), which no vector exercises. Correct statement: 'reproducing both fields for all 73 rows is a necessary condition; it does not cover 0x08, 0x00, or invalid-UTF-8 argv.'

verdicts.rule: All 73 rows are distinct (payload,secret) pairs producing 73 distinct signatures — there are no duplicate rows and no signature collisions, so a reimplementation cannot pass by emitting a constant.
verdicts.note: Reproduced: `awk -F'\t' '{print $1"\t"$2}' | sort | uniq -d` printed nothing, and `lines=73 distinct_sigs=73`. I also checked distinct full tokens: `awk -F'\t' '{print $4}' | sort -u | wc -l` -> 73. In the ctl file the two 'x'-payload rows (secrets `sec\tret` vs `sec\nret`) do yield different signatures (FraxoclAAoEvNqFVvlFj0B0cnP6doj6UP-DLQrhJZMY vs cFACDBorm5FZJS_HvmZ-74CRoBNUX34gd-eGWbEfK9E), confirming whitespace in the secret is significant.

verdicts.rule: Field 4 (full_token) always begins with the constant header segment 'eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9', which is base64url(no padding) of the exact bytes {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"} — key order alg then typ, no spaces. The header never varies with payload or secret.
verdicts.note: `awk -F'\t' '{split($4,a,"."); print a[1]}' /tmp/golden_vectors.tsv | sort -u` -> single line `eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9`. Decoding it (`tr '_-' '/+' | base64 -d`) gives exactly `{"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}` (27 bytes, alg before typ, no spaces); the segment is 36 chars. I could not vary it: empty payload, empty secret, 3000-byte inputs, non-ASCII, control bytes and invalid UTF-8 all produced the same first segment. It is also constant across the 9 ctl rows.

verdicts.rule: Segment 2 is base64url(no padding) of JSON {"data":<payload>} serialized with compact separators (',',':') and ensure_ascii=true: every non-ASCII codepoint becomes \uXXXX lowercase-hex, and astral-plane codepoints (e.g. emoji) become UTF-16 surrogate pairs \udNNN\udNNN. JS must NOT emit raw UTF-8 here.
verdicts.note: The original engineer's own evidence was inconclusive (their `base64 -d` output rendered as raw CJK/emoji, which literally contradicts their rule). I re-checked with od -c, which proves them right: `--payload='你好世界'` -> seg2 decodes to `{ " d a t a " : " \ u 4 f 6 0 \ u 5 9 7 d \ u 4 e 1 6 \ u 7 5 4 c " }` — six literal ASCII chars per escape, lowercase hex. `--payload='🎉'` (U+1F389) -> `{"data":"🎉"}`, i.e. a real surrogate pair. Also verified `é` -> é, U+FFFF -> ￿, U+2028 ->  , U+200B -> ​. No key ordering issue (single key). Bonus finding not in the rule: invalid UTF-8 bytes in the PAYLOAD survive via PEP-383 surrogateescape and appear as lone surrogates — `--payload=$(printf 'a\xffb')` gives seg2 `{"data":"a\udcffb"}` (rc=0). Standard JS JSON.stringify does emit \udcff for a lone surrogate, but the harness must decode argv with surrogateescape (byte 0xNN -> U+DCNN for invalid bytes) to get there.

verdicts.rule: CLI invocation rule for any harness re-running the executable: use the '--payload=VALUE' / '--secret=VALUE' equals form, not the space-separated form. Values beginning with '-' (rows 61 '-1e400', 68 '--payload'/'-secret', 69 '-'/'-') are rejected by argparse with exit code 2 under the space form, but succeed under the equals form. The two forms are otherwise byte-identical.
verdicts.note: The blanket claim 'values beginning with - are rejected under the space form' is false, and specifically the named row 69 ('-'/'-') is NOT rejected. `/workspace/dataset/test8_executable --payload - --secret -` -> rc=0, token `eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJkYXRhIjoiLSJ9.HNOFNeXxXpBZkyBftdQvha2WrPL_FgqMd7RoODx0lJE` (argparse treats a bare single '-' as a value, not an option). Negative-number-looking values are also accepted under the space form: `--payload -123 --secret k` -> rc=0 (`...eyJkYXRhIjoiLTEyMyJ9.7zcMhBV6Sq-YZNVZ_uMzmS6kmZ8jz_e_1Z_WOi6p69g`), `--payload -1.5 --secret k` -> rc=0, `--payload -0 --secret -42` -> rc=0. Corrected rule: under the space form a leading-'-' value is rejected UNLESS it is exactly '-' or matches argparse's negative-number pattern ^-\d+$ or ^-\d*\.\d+$. The practical advice (always use the equals form) is still sound. The 'otherwise byte-identical' half is CONFIRMED — I stressed it with '=' inside the value (`--payload='a=b=c' --secret='k=1'` vs the space form: identical tokens) and with empty values. Two undocumented behaviours a harness should know: argparse prefix abbreviation is enabled (`--pay=abc --sec=k` -> rc=0), and a repeated flag silently takes the last occurrence (`--payload=A --payload=B` == `--payload=B`).

verdicts.rule: On success the program writes exactly 3 LF-terminated lines to stdout and nothing to stderr, exit 0: line 1 = token, line 2 = Python dict repr of claims, line 3 = the constant "{'alg': 'HS256', 'typ': 'JWT'}". Only line 1 is captured in the golden TSV; lines 2-3 use Python repr (single quotes, ', ' separator, ': ' after key) and re-encode non-ASCII as raw UTF-8, NOT as \uXXXX.
verdicts.note: The structural half is CONFIRMED (3 LF-terminated lines, empty stderr, exit 0, line 3 always the constant `{'alg': 'HS256', 'typ': 'JWT'}`, only line 1 in the TSV). Two substantive errors in the repr characterization. (1) The VALUE is not always single-quoted. `--payload="it's" --secret=k` -> line 2 is `{'data': "it's"}` — Python repr switches to double quotes when the string contains ' but no ". With both quote characters it goes back to single quotes and backslash-escapes: `--payload='both'\''and"q'` -> `{'data': 'both\'and"q'}`. (Only the outer dict-key quoting and the `', '`/`': '` separators are truly constant.) (2) 'non-ASCII as raw UTF-8, NOT as \uXXXX' is false for any codepoint Python considers non-printable. Verified with cat -A: U+200B ZERO WIDTH SPACE -> `{'data': 'a​b'}`; U+00AD SOFT HYPHEN -> `{'data': 'a\xadb'}` (note the \xNN form, a third escape style the rule never mentions); U+2028 LINE SEPARATOR -> `{'data': 'a b'}`; a lone surrogate from invalid argv (`--payload=$(printf 'a\xffb')`) -> `{'data': 'a\udcffb'}`. Raw UTF-8 only appears for printable non-ASCII (`你好世界` -> `{'data': 'M-dM-=M- ...'}`, combining accents likewise). Correct rule: line 2 is Python `repr(dict)`, which emits raw UTF-8 only for codepoints where str.isprintable() is true, and \xNN / \uXXXX / \UXXXXXXXX otherwise, with quote style chosen per-string. Separately, the rule's implicit 'always exit 0 on success' hides a failure mode no vector covers: an invalid UTF-8 byte in the SECRET aborts. `--payload=x --secret=$(printf 's\xffk')` -> rc=1, empty stdout, and a stderr traceback ending `jose.exceptions.JWSError: 'utf-8' codec can't encode character '\udcff' in position 1: surrogates not allowed` plus `[PYI-13906:ERROR] Failed to execute script 'test8' due to unhandled exception!`. The same byte in the PAYLOAD succeeds (rc=0). The notes claim NUL is the only untestable input; invalid UTF-8 is testable and is the more interesting uncovered case.

verdicts.note: The HMAC block-size behaviour is CONFIRMED and I extended it: keylen 64/65/100/1000 of 'A' all match openssl (FcsGo0wOdsPqAXKtDGfCw6oST_udBp8neMyT1xj4Jzc / dIqx5PXuwoq_2NjPZjdQypuURY5lpJk8SXsX6jfF3gY / 7YzwAGUAygk1o-kG6VcBBDzF1gPDCPDjvfJc0wkyKUw / XkXN4eK4GD5s2TGl3rhFeUht22wGXGW9lGLkgi7si4o). BUT 'no error' is WRONG: python-jose rejects secrets whose bytes CONTAIN certain asymmetric-key markers, regardless of length. Counterexample at exactly 64 bytes: `K='ssh-rsaAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA'; ./test8_executable --payload hello --secret "$K"` -> EXIT=1, stdout EMPTY, stderr `jose.exceptions.JWKError: The specified key is an asymmetric key or x509 certificate and should not be used as an HMAC secret.` wrapped in `jose.exceptions.JWSError: <same message>` (jose/backends/cryptography_backend.py line 544 -> jose/jws.py 164/167 -> jose/jwt.py 63), while openssl -hmac with that key happily returns BKsi4x95I-XRgWC_XC6mYbFXP8n86WhfKsSIKPUhD5o. Full blocklist I mapped (case-sensitive SUBSTRING match anywhere in the secret; each verified exit=1): 'ssh-rsa', 'ssh-dss', 'ssh-ed25519', 'ecdsa-sha2-nistp256', 'ecdsa-sha2-nistp384', 'ecdsa-sha2-nistp521', and '-----BEGIN X-----' for X in {CERTIFICATE, X509 CRL, CERTIFICATE REQUEST, NEW CERTIFICATE REQUEST, TRUSTED CERTIFICATE, PUBLIC KEY, RSA PUBLIC KEY, PRIVATE KEY, ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY, RSA PRIVATE KEY, DSA PRIVATE KEY, EC PRIVATE KEY, DH PARAMETERS, OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY, SSH2 PUBLIC KEY}. Verified NOT blocked (exit 0): 'sshrsa', 'ssh_rsa', 'ssh-', 'ssh-rs', 'ssh-ds', 'ssh-dsa', 'ssh-ed448', 'ecdsa', 'ecdsa-sha2', 'ecdsa-sha2-', 'nistp256', 'rsa-sha2-256', 'SSH-RSA' (uppercase), '-----begin certificate-----' (lowercase), '-----BEGIN X-----', '-----BEGIN FOO KEY-----', '-----BEGIN AB-----', '-----BEGIN PKCS7-----', '-----BEGIN CMS-----', '-----BEGIN EC PARAMETERS-----', '-----BEGIN ATTRIBUTE CERTIFICATE-----', '-----BEGIN X509 CERTIFICATE-----', '-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE PAIR-----', '-----BEGIN DSA PUBLIC KEY-----', '-----BEGIN PARAMETERS-----', 'PUBLIC KEY', 'CERTIFICATE', 'x509'. Substring semantics proven with 'Zssh-dss' and 'ssh-dssZ' (both exit 1) and 'ecdsa-sha2-nistp256z' (exit 1). The blocklist applies ONLY to --secret: `--payload 'ssh-rsa -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- x'` exits 0 and serializes literally.

verdicts.note: The payload-side model is CONFIRMED and I strengthened it: I wrote my own model from scratch (/tmp/adv8/model.mjs, same escape table / literal range / lowercase 4-hex / base64url / HMAC rules) and ran 400 pseudo-random cases (/tmp/adv8/fuzz2.mjs) drawing payload chars from all of 0x01-0x7f plus U+0080/009F/00A0/00E9/00FF/0100/07FF/0800/2028/2029/3042/4E2D/D7FF/E000/FEFF/FFFD/FFFF/10000/1F600/10FFFF, and secrets from {'', 'k', 's3cret', non-ASCII, A*64, A*65, A*100, A*200, '~?+/=', two spaces, TAB+LF, U+00FF U+0100} -> `n=400 fail=0`. Also byte-identical on a 100000-char payload. BUT the model is NOT a full model of the program: it mispredicts every blocklisted or non-UTF-8 secret. Concretely, for secret 'ssh-rsa' the model emits eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJkYXRhIjoiaGVsbG8ifQ.Bo1hl55VqWnkHMMz4I6N0sCgrIeE0s2mxlsarpgbOXs while the executable exits 1 with 0 bytes of stdout; same for 'my-ssh-rsa-key' (model ...SjjEkEMCf7kj0fXGkK9QUDSMHvqa7PVFFlBLj5Gh4eQ vs exit 1) and for the raw-0xFF secret. Their fuzz never hit this because the secret was always 's'+length. A JS port must add the substring blocklist check and a strict-UTF-8 secret check before signing.

verdicts.rule: EDGE CASE: argv bytes that are not valid UTF-8 are decoded with surrogateescape and then serialized as LONE surrogates. Raw byte 0xFF in --payload yields {"data":"x\udcffy"} with exit 0 (no error).
verdicts.note: CONFIRMED for --payload: `./test8_executable --payload "$(printf 'x\377y')" --secret k` -> EXIT=0, segment eyJkYXRhIjoieFx1ZGNmZnkifQ, HEX=7b2264617461223a22785c756463666679227d = {"data":"x\udcffy"}, stderr empty. I extended the mapping: raw 0x80 -> \udc80; raw C0 80 -> \udcc0\udc80; raw ED A0 80 (CESU-style surrogate encoding) -> \udced\udca0\udc80 - i.e. each undecodable BYTE b maps to U+DC00+b and is emitted as its own \udcXX escape. BUT the rule is stated over 'argv bytes' generally, and that generalization is WRONG for --secret: `./test8_executable --payload hello --secret "$(printf 's\377k')"` -> EXIT=1, EMPTY stdout, `UnicodeEncodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't encode character '\udcff' in position 1: surrogates not allowed` -> `jose.exceptions.JWSError`. Correct rule: surrogateescape is survivable in --payload (because ensure_ascii turns the lone surrogate into a pure-ASCII \udcXX escape before the UTF-8 encode) but fatal in --secret (which is UTF-8-encoded strictly).
